newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe urges constitution reform for women.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe urges constitution reform for women.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe, branding French democracy lop-sided, called on Tuesday for "positive discrimination" to boost women's role in politics, which is among the weakest in the European Union.

Juppe told the National Assembly he personally favoured changing the constitution to allow quotas for women on lists of candidates for regional, municipal and European Parliament elections for a limited period of perhaps 10 years.

Opening a debate on parity in public life, Juppe said French laws guaranteeing sex quality had failed -- just 5.5 percent of deputies in the National Assembly are women and none of France's top 200 firms has a female boss.
A radio commentator quipped that that made the role of women in French public life only slightly better than in Afghanistan under the Taleban Islamist militia.

"I am convinced today that it's necessary to install positive discrimination," Juppe said. "I favour modifying our constitution". He urged "a real effort to catch up within the framework of what could be a 'decade of parity'."
He appealed for legislative proposals before the summer.

His suggestion for electoral quotas appeared to be an attempt to counter the opposition Socialist party, which has nominated 30 percent of women among its candidates for general election to the National Assembly in a year's time.

"Overall our democracy is completely lop-sided," Juppe said, noting that there were fewer women in parliament now than at the end of World War Two. "It only advances on one leg. It is leaving out more than half of our citizens."

Unlike the Socialist quota, Juppe's plan would not apply to the constituency system for elections to the National Assembly, where women have just 32 seats out of 577, the lowest percentage of any EU nation, or to the Senate (upper house). In the EU, women have most clout in Sweden, with 40 percent of seats.
Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said he favoured constitutional reform to help women but that Juppe was resigned to living with the problem in parliament for another decade.
"Our attitude is completely different. We're not waiting for the year 2007," he told France 2 television.
Ex-prime minister Laurent Fabius, the Socialist floor leader in the Assembly, said Juppe had tended to backtrack on womens' rights but that Socialists would judge reforms on their merits.
Juppe came to office in May 1995 after the election of President Jacques Chirac trumpeting a record 12 women in his cabinet, or 30 percent of ministers.

But he sacked eight of them in a reshuffle later that year, cutting women's percentage in the cabinet to an unexceptional 13 percent and drawing charges that the so-called "Juppettes" were a gimmick to help secure Chirac's election.
Fabius said that in 1997, fewer than 10 percent of 100 people nominated to top jobs by the cabinet were women.
Analysts said there was wide unease within the ruling coalition about the idea of reforming the constitution for women and that it was unclear if Juppe's suggestion would prevail.

France has had one female prime minister, Socialist Edith Cresson, who lasted a scant 10 months before resigning in 1992 with her popularity at a record low. She was the highest ranking woman since Joan of Arc led French armies in the 15th century.
Juppe noted that French women had only been given the vote after the Liberation from the Nazis in 1944, decades after many other European nations.

And the 19th century Napoleonic legal code gave men sweeping powers over their wives that lasted well into the 20th century. Juppe quoted Napoleon as saying a "woman was the property of man as a fruit tree belongs to a gardener".
